t.historic city of meknes@33.9,-5.6:
Meknes is the city of Moulay Ismail, a sultan who ruled Morocco for fifty-five years from 1672 and decided that the capital needed to be as big as his ambitions. He built an imperial city of ramparts, gates, palaces, granaries and stables, using thousands of workers and captives, and the scale of it still startles. Bab Mansour, the great ceremonial gate, is covered in green and white tilework and marble columns taken from Roman Volubilis, and it stands over a large square called El Hedim, where storytellers and food stalls gather in the evening. The granaries, the Heri es-Souani, are a series of immense vaulted halls with walls several metres thick, where grain and animals were once stored, and the quiet inside is cool and heavy.

Meknes is a city of more than half a million, with all the services, including fuel, pharmacies, cafes and repair shops, and it feels much less hurried than Fez, an hour to the east, or the tourist magnets of Marrakech. The medina is walkable and pleasantly local, and the wine from the surrounding vineyards is some of the best in Morocco. Parking near the main gates is reasonably easy, but in the old town you walk.

From Meknes the riding gets interesting. Thirty kilometres north lie the Roman ruins of Volubilis, with mosaics and a triumphal arch standing in wheat fields, and to the south the road climbs into the Middle Atlas toward El Hajeb, Ifrane and Azrou. The Middle Atlas is cedar country, with forests of huge old trees and Barbary macaques waiting beside the road for a handout, though feeding them is not a good idea. Ifrane, a ski town built in a Swiss-alpine style, feels completely out of place, which is rather the point.

The roads are generally good, with long bends, rolling highland and big skies, though trucks are slow on the climbs, and police radar is common, so keep to the limits. In winter the Middle Atlas gets snow and ice, with fog on the pass, and in summer it is a pleasant escape from the heat of the plains. Spring is the best season, with green fields, wildflowers and clear air, and autumn runs a close second.
t.tregonning and gwinear mining districts@:
Tregonning Hill is a low, rounded granite dome above Germoe, and on its slopes in the middle of the eighteenth century a Plymouth chemist named William Cookworthy found white clay of a quality that Europe had never produced. He recognised it as kaolin, the secret of Chinese porcelain, and the find began an industry that eventually shifted to the larger deposits around St Austell. The ground around Tregonning and Gwinear is a landscape of old tin and copper workings, engine houses, abandoned stacks and small fields enclosed by stone hedges. The whole Cornish mining landscape was listed by UNESCO in 2006 and these districts are part of it.

An engine house is the characteristic ruin of Cornwall, a tall, narrow building of granite with an arched window and a chimney stack beside it, built to house a beam engine that pumped water from the mine. The engines of Hayle, in particular, were exported across the world, from South Africa to Mexico, and Cornish miners went with them, which is why you can find pasties in Wisconsin and Cornish names in Australian mining towns. Hayle itself lies at the head of a sandy estuary, with dunes, a harbour, an old foundry and a busy beach, and a good place for a coffee. St Michael's Mount, a tidal island with a castle on top, rises from the bay to the south.

The riding in West Cornwall is slow, in the best sense. Lanes are narrow and sunken, with granite hedges and wild flowers on the banks, and they twist in tight bends through hamlets with names like Praze-an-Beeble. Surfaces can be patched and gritty, and meeting a tractor or a delivery van in a narrow stretch means reversing. In summer, the A30 and the coast roads are jammed with holiday traffic, so aim for spring or autumn, or for early mornings. The wind from the Atlantic is strong, and sea fog can roll in without warning.

Hayle has about eight thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets and bakeries, and Penzance is not far. Marazion and Uny Lelant are smaller. A pasty from a bakery, still warm, is the right lunch, and you eat it with your fingers. When the clouds clear, the late sun on the stone ruins makes them glow.
t.kennall vale@50.2,-5.2:
Kennall Vale is a steep, wooded ravine in the middle of Cornwall's mining country, and for a hundred years its stream was used to make gunpowder. The mills, built in the early nineteenth century, produced the powder that miners used to blast tunnels and shafts in the tin and copper mines, and the valley was chosen because it had water, privacy and trees to absorb explosions. The gunpowder works closed in the early twentieth century, and the buildings fell into ruin. Now the old mill walls stand in a thick green wood of oak, beech and ash, with moss on every stone and a leat, the stone-lined channel that brought the water, still threading through. It is one of the most atmospheric places in west Cornwall, and a nature reserve.

A walk through the vale takes forty minutes. Paths run along the stream, past a waterfall and the ruined mill houses, under tall trees and across stepping stones. After rain the stream is loud and brown, and the whole place drips. Bats roost in the ruins in winter, and in spring bluebells and wild garlic cover the ground. It is a place for a gentle pause rather than for a long visit. The vale is part of the UNESCO-listed Cornish mining landscape, because the gunpowder was as much a part of the industry as the engines.

The roads to the vale are narrow, deep lanes with high hedges, between small villages such as Stithians and Ponsanooth. They twist and rise in tight bends, with little visibility, and surfaces can be rough, so take them slowly. Tractors and delivery vans appear without warning, and in the lanes between the hedges a bike is an advantage. Stithians reservoir, close by, is a pretty stretch of water, and the village has a small shop.

Penryn, four kilometres away, has fuel and a few services, and the nearby port of Falmouth has everything, with a harbour, cafes and an excellent maritime museum. A pasty from a bakery is the right lunch. Wear boots, since the paths can be muddy, and bring a waterproof, because Cornish rain is fine and persistent. The best time is spring, when the wood is bright green.
t.cornwall and west devon mining landscape:
West Cornwall is the sort of place where a ruined engine house stands every few hundred metres, tall, square and roofless, with a chimney beside it. These are the remains of the tin and copper mines that made Cornwall one of the great industrial regions of the world in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The beam engines in these houses pumped water out of mines that went down hundreds of metres, in some cases under the sea. Miners from Cornwall, known as Cousin Jacks, took their skills around the globe, to Mexico, Australia, South Africa and the American Midwest, and the pasty went with them.

Around Camborne and Redruth, the heart of the mining district, the landscape is a patchwork of small fields, granite walls, heather and scrub, and the remains of workings that give the hills an odd texture. Richard Trevithick tried out his steam road locomotive in Camborne in 1801, and the great foundry at Hayle built engines that were shipped to mines everywhere. Hayle, six kilometres off, still has the tidal estuary, the dunes of the towans and a long, bright beach on the north coast.

Riding in Cornwall is a different thing from riding in the mountains. The roads are narrow, hedged and often sunken, with blind bends between granite banks, and you spend a lot of time slowing for tractors, caravans and holiday traffic. Out of season, though, the coast road between Portreath and Hayle is a good one, with views of the Atlantic and old mine stacks perched on the cliffs. The A30 is the fast road through the middle of the county, and gets crowded in July and August. Wet weather brings mud and diesel on the lanes.

Hayle has fuel, shops and cafes, and you will find pasties in every bakery. Truro and Penzance are within easy reach. Salt and wind are constant, and you can smell the sea in almost every village. Aim for May or September, when the light is clean and the crowds are thinner.
t.mosquee de nambira ou namboura missiri k:
In the north of Côte d'Ivoire, where the forest gives way to savanna, the villages are built of mud and every mosque looks like a sculpture grown out of the ground. They belong to the Sudanese style, a tradition from the Sahel that spread south along trade routes carried by Dyula merchants, and UNESCO listed several of them in 2021. The mosques of Kaouara, Kouto, Nambira, Tengrela and others are the survivors of that tradition in this country.

You can read how they work. The walls are earth, shaped into tapering buttresses that end in pointed pinnacles, and wooden beams stick out of the surface so that masons can climb to renew the mud plaster after each rainy season. Small windows keep the heat out and the sound in. Some towers have clay finials, and in other Sudanese-style buildings ostrich eggs sit on the points as symbols of fertility and purity. The result is part architecture, part sculpture, part annual community ritual, since the plastering is done by the villagers.

The riding is simple and hot. Roads through the savanna run past cashew orchards, maize fields, mango trees and villages of round and square houses, mostly on paved highway with rough patches and occasional laterite tracks in between. The rains from about May to October make the dirt soft, while the dry season brings harmattan dust that turns the horizon white-gold. Motorbikes are everywhere, usually overloaded, and people will happily wave you down for a chat.

There is no town in the nearby list, so plan to buy fuel at a larger regional town before you come, and carry water. Always ask permission before you photograph a mosque, since these are working places of worship, and be ready to take off your shoes if you go in. Women and visitors may be restricted from entering in some villages, which is a local decision, so a quiet look from outside is often the most respectful approach. Try to be here in the cool of early morning, when the colour of the walls is at its best.
t.wendron mining district@50.2,-5.2:
The first thing to know about Wendron is that the ground beneath it was once worked as hard as any in Europe. West Cornwall's tin and copper made the county rich, and the district around Wendron, a few kilometres north of Helston, was one of the places where it happened. The old mines, the stream works in the valleys and the engine houses on the hillsides are part of the Cornish Mining World Heritage Site, listed in 2006. Many of the ruins are hidden in woods or fields, so you will have to look for them.

The upland that stretches across the area is a mass of granite, the Carnmenellis, the source of both the tin and the stone that went into the farm buildings. The soil is thin, the hedges are stone banks topped with gorse, and the lanes between them are narrow, steep and winding, with a way of dropping suddenly into a stream valley and rising again with a hairpin. Many of these lanes have grass growing down the middle, and you need to approach blind corners at walking pace. In summer the verges are full of foxgloves, and in autumn the bracken turns the colour of rust.

Helston, with twelve thousand people, is the place for fuel and lunch. Each May it hosts the Flora Day, when the town fills with dancers in their best clothes and the Furry Dance winds through the streets and into the shops, a custom that goes back centuries. Stithians, a village to the north, has a reservoir with a popular sailing club, and Four Lanes, to the north-west, is a former mining village that now sits on the main road.

The weather in this part of Cornwall is mild but wet. Mist rolls in from the Atlantic, and the road can become slick with mud where tractors have been. Spring and early autumn offer the best chance of clear light, and the light on the old granite after rain is lovely. In July and August, the lanes are crowded with holiday traffic, and the coast is busy.

A cream tea or a pasty is the obvious meal, and a pint in a local pub, where the talk is of mining and weather, seems entirely natural.
Cornwall's mining history is told by its engine houses, and around Camborne and Redruth there are more of them than anywhere else. This was the richest square of country in the whole mining world in the nineteenth century, producing copper and then tin on a scale that made the district a global centre of mining technology. Engineers, pumps and steam engines were built here and exported to mines on every continent, and Cornish miners themselves, known as Cousin Jacks, emigrated to Australia, South Africa, Mexico and North America and took their skills with them.

Camborne was the home of Richard Trevithick, who built the first full-size steam carriage to carry passengers on the road in 1801 and drove it up Fore Street and Camborne Hill. The town celebrates him with a Trevithick Day in April, when steam engines parade through the streets. Above the towns, the hill of Carn Brea has a monument to a local landowner and the remains of an old castle, and from the top there is a view that takes in the north and south coasts at once.

The area is not pretty in a conventional way. Chimneys and engine houses stand in fields, rows of terraced houses climb the slopes, and the landscape has the hard-worn look of a place that has been dug over many times. But it has a weight of history, and a rider with an eye for it will enjoy it. The roads here are busy, with the A30 carrying holiday traffic, but the minor roads that cross the old mining ground are interesting, with sharp bends, granite walls and sudden views.

Camborne, with twenty-two thousand people, is a practical town with fuel, supermarkets and bakeries. Redruth, just up the road, is larger and has more of the same. Four Lanes, a small village between them, has a few shops.

This is a place for a pasty, which the county's miners ate underground, held by the crust and finished with a good deal of pepper. The weather is mild, and the sea air carries across the high ground. Spring and autumn are the best months, and the low sun on the old granite is good for photographs.
t.portreath harbour@50.3,-5.3:
Portreath is a harbour made by hand. Before the Bassets, the great landowning family of this part of Cornwall, built its quay in the late eighteenth century, there was only a cove between steep cliffs. Afterwards, there was a port that shipped copper ore to the smelters of Swansea and brought back coal, with a tramroad running up the valley to the mines. The tramroad, built in 1809, was one of the earliest in Cornwall, and horse-drawn wagons rolled down it for decades. The harbour has two basins, a sea wall, and a granite pier, and a rocky island called Gull Rock lies just off it.

The beach has golden sand and a good surf, and the village on summer weekends fills with surfers, families and campers. In winter, big Atlantic swells break against the harbour mouth, and watching them from the pier on a stormy day is an experience. The coast path runs along the cliffs on either side, and in spring the clifftops are covered in thrift and bluebells.

The ride from Redruth or Camborne comes down a steep valley, with a long hill into the village and tight bends. The coast road along the cliffs, the B3301, runs between Portreath and Hayle, with views of the sea and, on a clear day, the lighthouse at Godrevy. It is a popular route, so it is slow in high season, but quiet in early spring. The gravel and sand on the road near the beach can be tricky for a bike, so take care.

Redruth, with over forty thousand people in the urban area, and Camborne, a little smaller, both have fuel and supermarkets. The village has a few pubs and cafes, and the pasties and ice cream are good. Kennall Vale, on this ride, is a different place altogether: a wooded valley in the south of the county where gunpowder was made for the mines in the nineteenth century, and where the ruins of the mills lie among ferns and moss.

Late spring is the best season, with long evenings and wildflowers. Winter storms are dramatic but make the roads wet and slippery.
t.gwennap mining district@50.2,-5.2:
The hills between Redruth and Truro are some of the most worked ground in Europe. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Gwennap was said to be the richest square mile of mining country in the world, with copper and tin coming out of shafts so close together that the engine houses seem to stand shoulder to shoulder. Today the chimneys and roofless buildings stand in gorse and bracken, and the red-brown streams and spoil heaps tell you what lay underneath. The area is part of the Cornish Mining World Heritage Site, and the village of St Day, with about seven hundred people, sits at its centre, with a fine ruined church in the middle of a green.

Gwennap Pit is the odd gem. It is a round hollow, a collapsed mine working that was later turned into a grass amphitheatre, and John Wesley preached here from 1762 for decades to crowds of thousands. The terraces cut in the sides date from the nineteenth century, and the place still holds Methodist gatherings. Nearby Poldice Valley and Wheal Maid show how the landscape was altered by waste and wheel pits; the soil is poisoned in places, and walkers are asked to keep to the paths.

Riding is delightful and slow. Cornish lanes here are narrow, banked with hedges and often deep, so you ride with your eyes on the next bend and an ear for a tractor coming the other way. The A393 and A3047 are better surfaced and carry the traffic, but the real fun is in the back roads between St Day, Chacewater and Scorrier. After rain the surface is greasy, and in summer the lanes can be clogged with holiday traffic. Sea mist sometimes rolls in off the north coast, and it can feel cold on a bright morning.

Redruth, four kilometres away, has about forty thousand people and plenty of fuel and food, and the neighbouring town of Camborne holds the Camborne School of Mines. Chacewater has a pub and a shop. A proper Cornish pasty, with crimped edge and a filling of beef, potato, swede and onion, was designed to be eaten by miners with dirty hands, and you should buy one fresh. Take it up to the pit, if the weather is dry, and listen to the wind in the gorse.
t.tizi n tichka@31.3,-7.4:
The Tizi n'Tichka is the high road across the Atlas, the route that takes the main Marrakech to Ouarzazate highway over the crest of the mountains at about 2,260 metres. Below you, valleys of red earth and green terraced fields drop away toward the Sahara, and above you the bare slopes are patched with snow until late spring. In the Berber language tizi means pass, and the name has the sound of the wind itself.

Culture here is Amazigh, or Berber, a mountain people with ancient traditions of building in mud brick, weaving and farming on tiny irrigated terraces. Villages cling to slopes like extensions of the rock, their kasbahs flat-roofed and towered, in the same colour as the soil. Close to the pass a side road leads to Telouet, a huge kasbah of the Glaoui family, who ruled the region in the early twentieth century with French support, and whose crumbling halls still hold intricate plaster and tile work. Further on, the fortified village of Aït Benhaddou has featured in countless films.

The road itself was built by the French in the 1930s and is a delight and a trial, with continuous bends, hairpins and drop-offs on the southern side. Lorries crawl and sometimes block the narrow sections, and surfaces can be broken by frost and rockfall. Weather on the pass is serious: snow and ice can close the road in winter, and fog and rain can make it treacherous, so check conditions. Spring and autumn offer clear air, though a cold wind blows even in summer. Roadside stalls sell minerals, fossils and rugs.

Fuel is available in Marrakech and Ouarzazate, with some stations on the road between, but the stretch over the pass can be thin, so fill up before climbing. Small cafes at the top serve mint tea and tagine, and stopping for a warm drink is a good way to take in the views. Bargain gently with stallholders, who are friendly and persistent, and start early to avoid the afternoon lorries and the heat of the southern slopes.
t.cliffs of moher@53.0,-9.4:
The cliffs rise sheer out of the Atlantic for about eight kilometres along the west coast of County Clare, reaching just over two hundred metres at their highest point, and on a clear day the whole line of black shale and sandstone glows in the afternoon light. They are Ireland's most visited natural attraction, and they deserve it, although a good many of the visitors arrive by coach at the same hour, and the car park gets busy. The main viewing area is a small piece of the whole, and the further you walk along the coastal path, the quieter and wilder it becomes.

O'Brien's Tower, a round stone tower built on the cliff top in 1835 by a local landowner, Cornelius O'Brien, to give his Victorian visitors somewhere to enjoy the view, still stands and can be climbed. The modern visitor centre is tucked into the hillside, so that it hardly shows from the sea. At the southern end, Hag's Head is topped by an old signal tower, and legend has it that the shape of the headland resembles a woman's face looking out to sea. Puffins nest in the cliff top in spring and early summer, and thousands of seabirds, such as guillemots and razorbills, crowd the ledges.

Hold on to your helmet. The wind here can be strong enough to knock you off your feet, and sea mist sometimes closes the view altogether, so be ready for either. The cliff paths have fences in places, but beyond them are unprotected drops, and people have died by stepping too close. Keep well back from the edge.

The riding is good. The coastal road from Liscannor north toward Doolin has long views over the Atlantic, with the Aran Islands appearing offshore and the grey stone hills of the Burren rising inland, a unique limestone landscape of cracked pavement and rare flowers. Roads are narrow and winding, shared with tour buses and tractors, and surfaces can be rough after winter. Try to arrive early or late in the day to avoid the crowds. The nearest big town is Ennis, about thirty-three kilometres away, with fuel stations in nearer villages such as Lahinch and Ennistymon. Pubs in Doolin are famous for traditional music, and a bowl of seafood chowder is a fair reward for a day in the wind.
t.galway@53.3,-9.1:
Galway is a small city with a big personality, and most of that personality comes out on the street. It sits at the mouth of the River Corrib on the west coast of Ireland, with Galway Bay opening to the Atlantic and the hills of Connemara beginning just beyond the suburbs. It is known as the city of the tribes, after the fourteen merchant families who ran it in the Middle Ages, and a few of their house names, like Lynch and Blake, are still common in the area. The Spanish Arch beside the river is a reminder of the trade with Spain that brought wine and prosperity here.

The old streets are best on foot. Shop Street and the Latin Quarter fill with musicians, buskers, bookshops and pubs, and in the evening you can hear fiddles, flutes and bodhrans from several doors at once. Irish is spoken widely in the nearby Gaeltacht, and you will see bilingual signs everywhere. The Claddagh, a former fishing village at the river mouth, gave its name to the famous ring with two hands holding a crowned heart. Salthill, the seaside promenade a short distance west, has a long tradition of walking to the end and kicking the wall.

Food and festivals matter. The oyster festival in September draws visitors from all over to eat the local native oysters and drink stout, and the Galway Arts Festival in July fills the streets with street theatre and music. Seafood restaurants line the quays, and there are good bakeries and cafés on almost every corner.

The riding west from the city, along the Wild Atlantic Way through Spiddal and into Connemara, is lovely, with bog, lake and mountain scenery, white cottages and stone walls. Roads are generally narrow, though in decent condition, and the weather changes constantly, so waterproofs belong on the bike. Expect heavy traffic through the city centre, especially on weekends, and avoid it if you can. Fuel, repair shops and plenty of parking are available at the edges of the city. Whatever the weather, finish the day in a pub with a fire, and ask the barman what is on the music list.
t.achill island@54.0,-10.0:
Achill is Ireland's largest island, and you reach it by driving across a bridge, which takes a little of the romance away until you see the landscape. It lies off the coast of County Mayo, joined to the mainland at Achill Sound, and it is a rough, treeless land of heather bog, steep headlands and wide empty beaches. At Slievemore, the mountain that rises above the northern shore, a ruined village of stone cottages known as the deserted village stands on the slope, abandoned over generations after the Famine. At its foot, the winds sweep across the grass.

The coastline is spectacular. On the western side the cliffs of Croaghaun drop about seven hundred metres into the sea and are counted among the highest sea cliffs in Europe, though they are best seen from a boat or by hiking to the cliff top on a clear day. Keem Bay, at the far western end of the island, is a small curved beach of white sand and clear turquoise water, hemmed in by green hillsides, and approached by a steep, narrow road that is one of the most spectacular drives in Ireland. Basking sharks sometimes feed in the waters off Achill in early summer.

The German writer Heinrich Böll had a cottage on the island, and wrote about the place in his Irish Journal, which brought it to the attention of European readers. The Atlantic Drive, a circuit around the southern coast, climbs and dips past inlets and old stone walls, and the road is narrow, with plenty of sheep. The surface is generally fine but bumpy, and the wind is the main hazard, since a gust on an open headland can shift a loaded bike. The weather is changeable, with rain moving in from the Atlantic quickly.

Fuel is available at Achill Sound and in a couple of other villages, but stations are small, and the nearest large town is Westport, about thirty-seven kilometres to the east. Pubs and small restaurants serve seafood, lamb and brown bread, and the island is quiet in the evenings. The best months are May to September, when light lasts until late. Go up at sunset to the top of the road above Keem Bay, if the sky is clear, and watch the shadows move across the water.
t.ouarzazate@30.9,-6.9:
Ouarzazate is a town built where the High Atlas gives way to the desert, and the light there is so strong and clear that the film industry came to rely on it. It sits on a high plateau at the southern foot of the mountains, with the pale red earth and flat-topped hills of southern Morocco spreading out in front, and it has been the location for films such as Lawrence of Arabia, Gladiator and numerous others. Huge studio complexes on the edge of town offer visits, with sets of ancient Egypt and Tibet standing in the dust, but the real attraction lies in the kasbahs.

The Taourirt Kasbah, in the town itself, was the residence of the powerful Glaoui family, who ruled much of southern Morocco in the early twentieth century, and its mud-brick towers and intricately painted rooms give some idea of their wealth. About thirty kilometres away, the fortified village of Aït Benhaddou, a UNESCO site, rises on a hillside above a dry river, its towers and walls of clay glowing orange at sunset, and it is one of the best-preserved examples of southern Moroccan earthen architecture. Amazigh, or Berber, culture is strong here, and many people speak Tamazight as well as Arabic and French.

The famous ride is the road over the Tizi n'Tichka pass, which links Ouarzazate with Marrakech, about two hundred kilometres away. The pass crests at about 2,260 metres, and the road twists up the northern slope in long bends through villages of red mud houses, then drops down toward the dry south. The surface has been improved in recent years, but heavy trucks crawl up the climbs, and landslides or snow can close the road in winter. In summer it is hot in the lowlands and pleasantly cool at the top. Go early, since the light is best in the morning and the traffic is lighter.

Ouarzazate has fuel stations, workshops and plenty of hotels and cafés. In the evening, restaurants serve tagines and mint tea. Be aware of speed checks along the main road, which are common, and carry cash for small purchases. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with clear days and moderate temperatures, while July and August are very hot on the plains.
t.agadir@30.4,-9.6:
Agadir is a very new city in a very old country, and the reason is the earthquake. At a few minutes before midnight on 29 February 1960, a quake destroyed most of the old town and killed thousands of people, and the city was rebuilt from scratch in a modern style, with wide avenues, low buildings and a long promenade along the bay. The one piece that survived is the hilltop kasbah, Agadir Oufella, whose ruined walls overlook the town from about two hundred metres up, bearing an inscription in Arabic that reads God, Country, King. The view from it, across the bay and the port, is the best in town.

The beach is the main attraction, a long curve of pale sand backed by hotels and cafés, and it is busy with Moroccan families and European visitors. The weather is mild nearly all year, with a fresh Atlantic breeze that keeps summer temperatures bearable, and morning mist often rolls in from the sea. Behind the city lies the Souss valley, a fertile plain of orange groves and vegetable farms, bordered by the foothills of the Anti-Atlas, and the argan tree, found only in this part of Morocco, grows on the hills. Goats sometimes climb the trees to eat the fruit, which is pressed into oil by women's cooperatives.

For riders, the road north along the Atlantic is a joy. The coast road from Agadir toward Essaouira runs high above the sea, passing small fishing villages and surfing beaches such as Taghazout and Imsouane, and cutting through argan forests and cliffs, before reaching the white and blue walled port of Essaouira. The surface is mostly good, though sand blows over some sections, and there are many police checkpoints, so keep your papers handy and your speed legal. Strong winds are common, particularly in the afternoon, and mist can reduce visibility in the morning. Spring and autumn offer the best conditions, while summer is warm and busy.

Fuel is plentiful in the city and along the main roads, though it can be sparse on minor coastal tracks. Fresh sardines and grilled fish are the local specialty, served in simple restaurants near the port. Leave time for a late afternoon walk along the promenade and a glass of mint tea as the sun sets.
t.kinsale@51.7,-8.5:
Kinsale is a small harbour town on the south coast of County Cork, and it has been around long enough to have seen plenty of drama. The Battle of Kinsale in 1601 ended in defeat for the Irish lords and their Spanish allies and is often treated as the real end of the old Gaelic order. The star-shaped Charles Fort, built later in the seventeenth century, still guards the harbour mouth, and you can walk its ramparts for a view across the water.

For a rider, Kinsale is the traditional start of the Wild Atlantic Way, a signposted route that follows the west coast of Ireland northward for well over two thousand kilometres. The town itself has narrow streets lined with colourful shops, bars and restaurants, and it has a reputation across Ireland as a food town, with a strong tradition of seafood and a gourmet festival that has run for decades. The Bandon river meets the sea here, and in good weather the harbour full of small boats makes for an easy half hour.

The road out is more gentle than dramatic. The country lanes around Kinsale are narrow and twisting, with high hedges and little forward visibility, so it pays to ride well within yourself and expect a tractor or a van around any corner. Surfaces in Ireland can be rough and patched, especially at the edges, and rain arrives quickly off the Atlantic, so a waterproof layer is not optional. On a clear spring or early summer morning, though, it is very pleasant, and the coastline to the west opens up quickly.

Fuel is the one thing to plan. Kinsale is a town of a few thousand and does have a station, but larger supply and more choice lie at Carrigaline, about fifteen kilometres away, and at Bandon, a similar distance inland. Fill up before heading west, because the route out toward Clonakilty and beyond has long gaps between towns.

Come for a pint and a plate of fish, stay for the evening light on the harbour, and set off early the next day when the town is still asleep.
t.mizen head@51.5,-9.8:
Ireland runs out here, and it does so with a flourish. Mizen Head is the south-western tip of the island, a ragged headland of dark rock and heather above a sea that is rarely calm, and the road ends at the point where there is nothing between you and Newfoundland but ocean. From the clifftop you can see the Fastnet Rock far out to the south-west, a lonely pinnacle with a lighthouse, which was the last sight of Ireland for many emigrants and is often called Ireland's Teardrop.

The way here is long and slow. From Durrus or Schull you follow narrow regional roads through Goleen and Crookhaven, past stone walls, whitewashed cottages and fuchsia hedges that glow red in late summer. The surface is patchy, the road is often single track with passing places, and the corners are blind, so you need to ride with the expectation of a tractor around every bend. Do not expect to hurry. The reward is the changing light, with the sea turning from slate to turquoise as clouds move across, and the sudden glimpse of white beach at Barleycove, where dunes and a lagoon sit in a gap in the cliffs.

The old signal station at the end of the point has been turned into a visitor centre, reached by a footbridge across a deep gully, with the sea churning white beneath it. The station was built to give mariners a weather report and to watch for ships in trouble, and the arched concrete bridge, completed in the early twentieth century, is a fine piece of engineering. The cliffs here are full of seabirds, and if you are lucky you may see whales or dolphins out at sea, especially in late summer. Opening times for the visitor centre vary with the season, so check before you go.

Be realistic about supplies. There is little fuel on the peninsula, and the nearest big towns are Bantry and Skibbereen, so fill the tank before you commit. Cafes at Crookhaven and Goleen are small but welcoming, and in summer a bowl of chowder and brown bread is the right thing. Weather is the great variable. A calm bright day here is a rare joy, but the wind can be ferocious, so take a good jacket whatever the forecast says. Spring and early autumn are quieter than high summer.
t.slieve league@54.6,-8.7:
Slieve League is one of the tallest sea cliffs in Europe, and it is a very different thing from the more famous cliffs on the other side of the country. The mountain drops about six hundred metres straight into the Atlantic, in bands of red, yellow and grey rock that look like a painter's palette in clear light. From the viewpoint at Bunglass, you look along a curtain of cliff that is far taller than anything you have seen on the coast of Clare, and the sound of the sea reaches you from a very long way down.

The road to it is the real adventure. From the village of Carrick, you take a narrow lane that climbs steadily through bog and heather, past a small lake, with the Atlantic spread out below to the left. Gradients are steep in places, the surface is rough and the road is often single track, and when it is busy you may have to wait at passing places. In clear weather the view over Donegal Bay is huge, with Sligo's flat-topped Benbulben visible on the far side. In fog, which comes in quickly, the road becomes a wet tunnel, so choose a clear day.

The area is part of the Donegal Gaeltacht, where Irish is still spoken every day, and you will notice the signs are in Irish first. The little village of Teelin below the cliffs was a fishing harbour, and an old pilgrimage route climbs the mountain to a ruined chapel on the shoulder. The path known as One Man's Pass, a narrow ridge with a drop on both sides, is only for experienced walkers and in good weather.

Fuel is the sticking point. Killybegs, about fifteen kilometres away, is Ireland's biggest fishing port and has stations and cafes, and it is where the large trawlers dock, which gives the harbour a lively industrial feel. Donegal town and Ardara are the other options. Bring waterproofs even in summer, because the weather here can change in minutes. Spring and early autumn bring clearer light and fewer visitors, and the evening sun on the cliffs, in September, is one of the great sights of the north-west.
t.kenmare@51.9,-9.6:
Kenmare sits at the head of a long sea inlet, with mountains on both sides and the Kerry hills rolling away to the north, and it is one of the best-placed small towns in Ireland. It was laid out as a planned town in the late eighteenth century by the Lansdowne estate, and the streets still form a tidy shape around a central market place, with colourful shopfronts, craft shops and some of the best restaurants in the south-west. Because it stands where the Ring of Kerry meets the Beara Peninsula, it is a natural starting point for either.

Fuel and food are easy here. With just over two thousand people, Kenmare has several petrol stations, banks, supermarkets and plenty of cafes, and in summer the streets are full of visitors. If you are heading out around the Ring of Kerry, remember that coaches are asked to go anticlockwise, so if you ride the same way you will often be stuck behind them, while riding clockwise tends to be quieter. The N71 east to Killarney crosses Moll's Gap, one of the most dramatic stretches in the south-west, with views over the Kerry mountains and the lakes.

On the edge of town, beside the road, lies a stone circle that is one of the largest in south-west Ireland, fifteen standing stones laid out around a big boulder in the middle. Nobody knows exactly why it was built, but it is thought to be about three thousand years old, and standing inside it with a bike ticking quietly behind you is worth a few minutes. Kenmare also has a long tradition of lacemaking, introduced by nuns in the nineteenth century, and the town's history includes the dark years of the Famine, when the workhouse was crowded.

Out of town, the Beara road west, along the south side of the bay, is quiet, twisting and beautiful, with the water on one side and the hills on the other. The Healy Pass, which climbs steeply between Kerry and Cork in tight hairpins, is a few kilometres further on and is one of the great rides in Ireland. Weather rolls in off the Atlantic, so be prepared for rain, but when the sun comes out the water in the bay turns a deep blue and the hills glow green. Late spring and September are the quietest and most reliable months.
t.bru na boinne archaeological ensemble of:
Brú na Bóinne means the bend of the Boyne, and the loop of the river that gives it its name holds one of the most important prehistoric landscapes in Europe. Three great passage tombs, Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth, stand on a low ridge above the water, built by farmers about five thousand years ago. That makes them older than Stonehenge and older than the pyramids of Giza, a thought that tends to silence even the chattiest visitor.

Newgrange is the one most people come to see. A great round mound faced with white quartz, it hides a long stone passage and a chamber with a corbelled roof, and at dawn on the winter solstice a shaft of sunlight enters through a small opening above the door and slowly lights the floor of the chamber. The builders aligned it with deliberate care. Knowth, nearby, is surrounded by smaller mounds and holds the largest collection of megalithic art in Europe, with spirals and zigzags carved on its kerbstones.

Access is organised through a visitor centre on the south bank of the river, from where a bus takes visitors to the monuments, and booking ahead is essential in summer. The village of Slane, about five kilometres away, is small, with a famous castle that has hosted rock concerts, a bridge over the Boyne and a few pubs. Drogheda, a larger town of over 33,000 people, lies nine kilometres to the east and is the place for fuel and supplies. Not far from here, in 1690, the armies of William of Orange and James II fought the Battle of the Boyne.

The roads of the Boyne valley are gentle and green, winding between hedges and low hills, and the riding is relaxed rather than thrilling. Rain is common, and the roads can be slippery. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn, when the light is soft. A visit takes a couple of hours, and a pint in Slane afterwards is the natural end.
t.mosquee de kaouara@10.1,-5.2:
The mosque at Kaouara looks as though it has grown from the earth, and in a sense it has. It is one of a group of Sudanese-style mosques in northern Côte d'Ivoire, built of mud brick over timber frames, with tapering buttresses and wooden beams that stick out of the walls like quills. These beams serve as permanent scaffolding, which allows the community to climb up each year and replaster the surface with fresh mud. UNESCO added the group to the World Heritage list in 2021, recognising a building tradition that came down the trade routes from the old Mali Empire.

The mosques here date from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries and were built by Muslim traders and scholars who travelled along the caravan roads between the savanna and the forest. The style is spare, with solid walls, narrow openings, and a pair of conical towers topped with clay pots or ostrich eggs. Inside it is dark, cool and quiet. Visitors should dress modestly, ask permission, and remember that these are active places of worship, not museums.

The landscape is the Sudanese savanna: open woodland, tall grass, shea trees and baobabs, with red laterite soil and villages of round or square mud houses. Riding here means laterite tracks and patchy tarmac, with long stretches of dust in the dry season. The harmattan, a dry wind from the Sahara, brings a haze between December and February, and from May to October heavy rains turn tracks into mud and can make some routes impassable. Mornings are the best time for riding, before the heat becomes strong.

Fuel can be a challenge away from the main towns, and I cannot say which village has a pump. The larger centres of the north, such as Korhogo and Ferkessédougou, are the sensible places to refuel and to find rooms. Carry spare fuel, plenty of water and cash in West African francs. Greet villagers properly, accept the offer of shade if it comes, and let a local guide show you where to find the keeper of the mosque.
t.boumalne dades@31.4,-6.0:
The road to Boumalne Dadès runs through country that looks like another planet. The town sits at about fifteen hundred metres on the edge of the High Atlas, on the old route known as the Road of a Thousand Kasbahs, and from here the Dadès river cuts a gorge into red rock that is among the finest in Morocco. The settlement itself is small and dusty, a stop on the highway with a market, cafes and a handful of hotels, but it is the gateway to some serious riding.

The gorge is the big attraction. The road runs north along the river past orchards and fortified villages built of mud and straw in the colour of the earth, and then climbs into the narrows, where cliffs close in. A set of tight hairpins at Tamellalt climbs a steep face in a tight zigzag that riders love, and a short distance on, strange eroded rock pillars known as the Monkey Fingers rise above the road. Surfaces are generally good but narrow, with sand and gravel on the bends, and landslides or flash floods can close sections after rain.

The people here are Amazigh, the Berber inhabitants of the mountains, and their culture shows in the weaving, the architecture and the language. Tea with mint and plenty of sugar is offered as a sign of welcome, and a tagine of lamb and vegetables cooked in a clay pot is the standard meal. About twenty kilometres west, Kelaat M'Gouna is the centre of the rose harvest, and in May the town holds a festival to celebrate it, with rose water, soap and perfume sold in the shops.

Boumalne Dadès has fuel, though it is wise to fill up whenever you can in the south, and Kelaat M'Gouna has more services. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, since summer heat can be fierce and winter nights are cold, with snow on the passes. The light in the gorge in late afternoon, when the cliffs turn deep red, is something to stay for.
t.sally gap@53.1,-6.3:
Sally Gap is a bleak crossroads in the middle of the Wicklow Mountains, about 495 metres above sea level, where the road from Dublin meets the one running across the hills from Glendalough to Roundwood. There is nothing there but a signpost, a sheep or two on the tarmac and a view of huge, rolling bog under a sky that seems to change every ten minutes. It is the sort of place that feels at the edge of the world, although the centre of Dublin is only about forty minutes away.

The road itself, the Military Road, was built in the early nineteenth century after the 1798 rebellion, when the British wanted to open up the hills where rebels had been hiding. It runs south from the village of Glencree along the flank of Kippure, and you pass the Glencree valley, once home to a barracks. Near the gap, you can look down on Lough Tay, a dark lake in a steep-sided bowl that is nicknamed the Guinness Lake, thanks to the pale sand on one shore and the peaty black water, and it is part of the Luggala estate owned by the Guinness family. The River Liffey rises on the slopes of Kippure close by and begins its long run to Dublin Bay.

The surface is generally good, with long views, easy sweeping bends and a few dips, but there is no shelter, and wind and fog can arrive without warning. Sheep wander on the road at will, so slow down, particularly on blind crests. In winter, ice and snow can close the road. In summer, weekends bring a steady stream of cyclists, walkers and cars, and the best time to ride is early morning or on a weekday evening.

Enniskerry and Bray lie to the north, and Roundwood to the south has a few shops and pubs. The hills are part of Wicklow Mountains National Park, with heather, blanket bog and a surprising number of red grouse, and the view back down to the lowlands on a clear day is worth the climb.
t.taghazout@30.5,-9.7:
Taghazout started as a fishing village and still smells like one around the harbour at dawn, but since the late sixties it has had a second life as Morocco's surf town. Travellers on the hippie trail drifted up the coast from Agadir looking for empty point breaks, and the names they gave the waves, Anchor Point and Killer Point among them, stuck. Today the village climbs a hillside above the Atlantic in tiers of whitewashed and sand-coloured houses, with surf schools and rooftop cafes in between the older family homes, and a large resort development now sits in the bay to the north.

For a rider this is where the coast road starts to behave. South of here you have spent the morning in the traffic and roundabouts of Agadir, which is a big city of nearly seven hundred thousand and the place to fill the tank properly before you leave. North of Taghazout the road bends along the cliff edge, drops to small coves, then climbs again, with the western end of the High Atlas running down to meet the ocean on your right. The surface is generally decent, but sand blows across the tarmac in places, and an Atlantic fog can sit on the cliffs until mid-morning, so the best light and the best grip come after ten.

Stop for a mint tea or a plate of grilled sardines and look at what the locals are doing rather than the tourists. The fishermen still land their catch on the beach, and in the evening the whole village drifts down to watch the swell. Beyond the village the hills fill up with argan trees, a gnarled, thorny species that grows almost nowhere else on earth, and in season you will see goats standing in the branches eating the fruit, a sight that is real and not only a postcard trick, although the ones beside the road are often there for the tips.

Plan the day around the wind. The coastal trade wind builds in the afternoon, especially in summer, and a loaded bike on an exposed headland feels it. Taghazout itself is a good place to rest, with plenty of simple guesthouses, and the sunsets over the water are good enough to justify staying a night instead of pressing on to Tamri and Essaouira.
t.exmouth@-21.9,114.1:
Exmouth is a long way from anywhere, and that is the whole point. The town sits near the tip of the North West Cape in Western Australia, where the Coral Coast Highway runs out of continent, with the Indian Ocean on one side and the shallow Exmouth Gulf on the other. From Carnarvon it is a full day of red dirt, scrub and sky, and when the first sign of the Cape Range appears on the horizon you feel genuinely rewarded.

The town is younger than most riders expect. It was founded in the late 1960s to house people working at the naval communications station on the cape, a Cold War installation that still sends very low frequency signals to submarines, and a forest of tall masts is visible from many points on the peninsula. The residents have since turned to tourism, fishing and prawning, and the main street has a relaxed, sun-baked feel.

What draws people is Ningaloo, a fringing coral reef that comes almost to the beach. Unlike the Great Barrier Reef, you can wade in from the sand with a snorkel and find yourself among parrotfish and coral within a few strokes. From about March to July whale sharks gather offshore, and from June to November humpback whales pass through. On the other side of the road, Cape Range National Park rises in dry limestone gorges where black-footed rock-wallabies cling to ledges, and the road along the coast to Yardie Creek is sealed and easy, with emus and kangaroos along the verge, especially in the evening.

On the bike, the main hazards are distance, wind and wildlife. Crosswinds on the open plains can be strong, kangaroos and emus are most active at dawn and dusk, and the heat from November to March is severe. Fuel and food are available in Exmouth, which is a proper town with a supermarket and workshops, but stations on the way up are far apart, so check your range before leaving the last one.

Ride out to the Vlamingh Head lighthouse near sunset: the view over the reef and the ocean as the colours deepen is worth the short, bumpy approach.
t.belfast@54.6,-5.9:
Belfast is a Victorian industrial city that has spent the last few decades reinventing itself, and it is worth giving yourself a morning here before you head out. The Lagan river runs through the middle toward Belfast Lough, and on its banks stand the two enormous yellow cranes of the Harland and Wolff shipyard, known as Samson and Goliath, where the Titanic was built and launched in 1911. The area around them is now the Titanic Quarter, with a big museum shaped like the prow of a ship. The city's other great landmark is the hills; Cave Hill, whose cliff face is said to have inspired Swift's idea of a sleeping giant, rises right behind the north of the city.

Politics and history are everywhere here, and visitors who take a walking or taxi tour of the murals will understand a lot about the Troubles and the peace that came after. Away from that, the Cathedral Quarter and the city's pubs are lively, with live music most nights and food that has become genuinely good. Stop for an Ulster fry if you are hungry; it is the sort of breakfast that sets you up for a long ride.

For motorbikes, Belfast is the start of the Causeway Coastal Route, one of the best roads in the British Isles. You leave north along the A2 through Carrickfergus, with its Norman castle, and then follow the coast of Antrim past Larne and the Glens, with the sea on one side and green hills on the other. It is a big road, sometimes slow behind lorries and tourists, but rewarding in clear weather, with the Scottish coast visible across the water on good days. Rain comes in fast, so be ready.

Fuel and food are no trouble in a city of this size, with filling stations on all the major roads out. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, particularly on the Westlink and the M2, so aim to leave between nine and ten. You will find plenty of secure parking near the city centre, and many of the hotels have bike spaces.
t.newquay@50.4,-5.1:
Newquay is the surf capital of England, though it started as something humbler. The name means new quay and goes back to the fifteenth century, when a harbour was built to replace an older one, and for a long time pilchards were the business. On the headland above the harbour stands the Huer's Hut, where a lookout watched for shoals and shouted to the fishermen through a megaphone. Victorians then brought the railway and the first visitors, and in the 1960s surfers arrived with boards from Australia and California.

Today the town is a mixture of cheerful surf culture and the noise of hen parties, with long golden beaches, Fistral and Watergate Bay among them, backed by hotels, caravan parks and cliff paths. In August the Boardmasters festival brings tens of thousands to the area, and the roads clog completely, so avoid that week unless you are going for the music. Outside the peak, it is much more pleasant, with a relaxed seaside atmosphere and good light on the water in the evenings.

The A39, the Atlantic Highway, is the long road that follows the north Cornish and Devon coast, and Newquay is a natural place to finish a day on it. The road itself is a mixture of fast open stretches over the high ground and slow sections through villages, with some lovely views of the sea and the headlands. Around Newquay, the A3058 and A392 are busy in summer and not much fun behind caravans, and the best riding is on the small roads north toward Padstow and Trevose Head, or south along the cliffs to Perranporth. Sea fog can drift in quickly and make the road slick.

With about twenty thousand people, Newquay has plenty of fuel, and every sort of food from pasties to fish and chips. Pasties are the right answer for a rider; buy one hot, eat it on the harbour wall, and watch the surfers. Parking a bike in the town centre is usually easy, though cheaper on the edges, and there are secure spots at several hotels.
t.dungarvan@52.1,-7.6:
Dungarvan lies at the head of a sheltered bay on the south coast of County Waterford, where the Colligan river meets the sea. The Normans built a castle here in the late twelfth century, said to have been ordered by King John, and its stone walls still stand beside the quay with a nearby barracks. The town takes its name from the Irish Dún Garbhán, and the Gaeltacht of An Rinn, where Irish is the daily language, lies just across the bay, giving the area an unusual sense of living tradition.

The Copper Coast, which stretches west from Tramore to Stradbally, gets its name from the old mines that once worked the cliffs. It is a European Geopark, with sea stacks, coves and ancient volcanic rocks, and the cliff road gives views of fields running to the edge and white surf below. Inland, the Comeragh Mountains rise to bare, hollowed corries and a big lake called Coumshingaun, and the roads that cross them are quiet and dramatic. A long disused railway between Dungarvan and Waterford has been turned into a greenway for cyclists and walkers, crossing viaducts and a tunnel.

For a rider, Dungarvan is a satisfying place to end a day. The coastal roads east from Tramore and west toward Youghal are generally good, with plenty of bends and flat, open stretches, and in clear weather the light over the bay is lovely. The N25 is the main road and carries a lot of lorries and holiday traffic, so the quieter R675 along the coast is better. Rain comes in off the Atlantic, often in short heavy showers, and the roads can be greasy. Watch for tractors, cyclists and the occasional herd of cattle crossing.

Fuel is easy in a town of seven and a half thousand, with several stations and supermarkets. Eat seafood at one of the harbourfront pubs; fresh haddock and chips or a bowl of chowder are the sensible choices, and a pint of stout fits any weather. Many guesthouses and B&Bs welcome motorcyclists and will find a dry spot for your bike. Walk across the bridge to Abbeyside in the evening, when the lamps come on, and look back at the castle.
t.tralee@52.3,-9.7:
Tralee is the county town of Kerry and the gateway to the Dingle Peninsula, and for one week each August it turns into a festival town. The Rose of Tralee, an international beauty and talent contest founded in 1959 and based on a nineteenth-century love song, draws women of Irish descent from around the world, and the whole town fills with music and crowds. Outside festival time, it is a busy, practical market town of about twenty-three thousand people, a place for supplies and a pint.

The town has some interest. At Blennerville, just outside, a restored windmill from about 1800, said to be the largest working windmill in Ireland, stands beside the old harbor from which thousands of emigrants sailed for America in the nineteenth century. The Kerry County Museum tells the story of the region, and the Siamsa Tíre theater celebrates traditional music and dance. The long beach at Banna and the sea cliffs beyond are a short ride away, and Tralee Bay sparkles in good weather.

For riders, Tralee is the start of one of the best rides in Ireland. The N86 runs west past the head of Tralee Bay and over the shoulder of the Slieve Mish mountains to Dingle town, and the classic way back is over the Conor Pass, at about 410 meters among the highest in Ireland, with sheer drops and tight hairpins. Beyond Dingle, the Slea Head loop circles the western tip, with views of the Blasket Islands and Atlantic swells. The roads are narrow, often with no edge line, and in summer tourist buses and campervans clog them, so early starts and patience are essential.

Tralee has everything: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels. Castleisland and Killorglin are smaller. The best months are May, June and September, when the light is long and the crowds are fewer. Weather on the Atlantic coast is changeable, with rain and wind a constant possibility, and fog can close the Conor Pass in minutes. In winter, storms make the peninsula wild. Sheep and cattle are often on the road, so slow down at blind corners.
t.dublin@53.3,-6.2:
Dublin is a city on a river and a bay, with a mountain range that starts within a short ride of the quays. The Liffey divides it into north and south, spanned by a string of bridges, and the Georgian squares, the cobbles of Temple Bar and the great Guinness brewery at St James's Gate give the place its character. Brick houses with fanlights and colored doors line the streets, and the pubs, bookshops and literary landmarks are a tribute to writers such as Joyce, Yeats and Wilde.

For a rider, the interest is what lies south. Within half an hour of the center, the Dublin Mountains rise, and beyond them the Wicklow Mountains, a huge upland of heather, bog and granite that stretches down the coast. The Military Road, built by the British after the 1798 rebellion to hunt rebels in the hills, climbs over Sally Gap, at about 500 meters, through a bleak, beautiful high moor, passing the dark lake of Lough Tay, nicknamed the Guinness Lake for its pint-black water and creamy sand beach. Farther south, the Wicklow Gap road crosses another pass, past the monastic ruins of Glendalough, founded in the sixth century by St Kevin.

The riding is excellent: wide, empty moorland, long views, gentle curves and a surface that is mostly good, though sheep wander the roads and the weather can change quickly. Weekends are busy, with cyclists, walkers and day-trippers from the city, so weekday mornings are best. Fog and low cloud can cover the high roads in minutes, and the wind across the bog is cold even in summer.

Dublin has every service, though traffic and parking in the center are difficult, and a ride south needs to avoid the rush hour on the M50 ring road. Fuel stations are everywhere, and Rathmines and Ringsend are inner suburbs with plenty of shops. The best months are May to September, with long evenings, though Irish rain can come at any time. Winter brings ice on the high roads, which can close them. Watch the speed limits, which are lower in Ireland than many riders expect and are enforced with cameras.
t.drogheda@53.7,-6.3:
Drogheda stands on the River Boyne, a short way from where the river meets the Irish Sea, and its position made it a frontier town for centuries. The old walled town, with its steep streets and the St Laurence's Gate, a medieval barbican, was one of the main ports of the Pale, the English-controlled district around Dublin. In 1649, Oliver Cromwell's army stormed the town, and a massacre of the garrison and civilians followed, a memory that still carries bitterness.

A more peaceful relic sits in St Peter's Church, where the preserved head of St Oliver Plunkett, the archbishop executed in London in 1681, is displayed in a shrine. Millmount Fort, a hill overlooking the town, houses a museum and gives views across the rooftops and the river, and the great railway viaduct across the Boyne is a landmark. Just upstream, the Battle of the Boyne was fought in 1690, when William of Orange defeated James II, a victory that shaped Irish history.

The Boyne Valley beyond is the real treasure. At Brú na Bóinne, just west of Drogheda, the great passage tomb of Newgrange, built around 3200 BC, older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, has a roof box that lets the winter solstice sun shine down its long passage. Nearby, Knowth and Dowth are similar mounds. Monasterboice, north of town, has a round tower and the tall carved high crosses of the early monastery, and Mellifont Abbey, founded in 1142, was the first Cistercian house in Ireland.

For riders, the lanes of the valley are gentle and green, with old stone bridges, hedgerows and cattle, and the main roads are fast, with the tolled M1 motorway running north-south beside. The surface is mostly fine, though country lanes are narrow, with tractors and farm vehicles. Drogheda has fuel, supermarkets, pubs and restaurants. The best months are May to September, though the winter solstice is the day to be at Newgrange, with a lottery for places. Rain is likely at any time, so pack waterproofs.
t.ballymena@54.9,-6.3:
Ballymena sits in the middle of County Antrim on the River Braid, a brisk market town of nearly thirty thousand people that most riders meet as a roundabout on the way to somewhere prettier. That undersells it a little. The town grew rich on linen in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and the Scots-Irish settlers who came here left a dialect and a stubborn Presbyterian streak that you can still hear in the shops. Buses are the modern trade: the big coachbuilder on the edge of town ships its vehicles round the world.

For a rider, Ballymena is a staging post, and a good one. Every kind of fuel is available without fuss, and the high street has the usual bakeries and coffee counters if you need to warm up. Remember that Northern Ireland prices fuel in pounds and measures speed in miles per hour, which catches out visitors coming up from the Republic.

The reason to stop here is what lies on either side. To the east the land lifts to the Antrim plateau, and the road to Broughshane leads towards the cone of Slemish, the old volcanic plug where, according to tradition, the teenage Patrick tended sheep as a slave. To the north-east the Glens of Antrim open up, nine deep valleys cut into basalt and fed by peaty streams, with Glenariff the one most people ride. The surface on these B-roads is variable, patched after hard winters, and the sheep own the verges.

Weather here is the Atlantic kind: four seasons in an afternoon, with squalls arriving off the Sperrins in the west and the light turning brilliant ten minutes later. Late spring and early autumn give the best mix of dry tarmac and low traffic. Summer weekends can be busy on the coast road at Cushendall and Waterfoot, so go early and ride the glens first.

If you are heading for the Giant's Causeway, Ballymena is a sensible place to tank up and eat a proper lunch before the tourist coaches begin to crowd the north coast. Treat it as a base rather than a destination and it will do the job well.
t.carrickfergus@54.7,-5.8:
Carrickfergus has a Norman castle that has been standing guard over Belfast Lough for more than eight hundred years, and it is a fine place to begin a ride along the Antrim coast. John de Courcy, an Anglo-Norman adventurer, built it in the 1170s after seizing a swathe of Ulster, and the stout keep, curtain walls and gatehouse have survived sieges, bombardments and centuries of garrison life. It is among the best-preserved medieval castles in Ireland, and it sits right on the shore, with waves lapping at the rocks and ferries and ships passing in the lough beyond.

William of Orange landed here in June 1690 on his way to the Battle of the Boyne, and a plaque and a statue on the quayside mark the spot. The town is also the ancestral home of the parents of Andrew Jackson, the seventh president of the United States, and a small cottage of the Ulster-Scots tradition is preserved nearby. t.healy pass@51.7,-9.8:

t.castletownbere@51.7,-9.9:

t.allihies@51.6,-10.0:

t.glengarriff@51.8,-9.6:

t.killorglin@52.1,-9.8:

t.molls gap@51.9,-9.7:

t.tramore@52.2,-7.2:

t.dunmore east@52.2,-7.0:

t.bunmahon@52.1,-7.4:

t.dublin@53.3,-6.3:

t.glenmacnass waterfall@53.1,-6.3:

t.laragh@53.0,-6.3:

t.tizi n test@30.9,-8.4:

t.el jadida@33.2,-8.5:
