t.kenmare food@51.9,-9.6:
Kenmare is the tidy, well-fed town at the head of the bay of the same name, in the south-west corner of County Kerry, and it is one of those places where a stop for lunch tends to turn into an afternoon. The streets are laid out in the shape of an X, with colourful shopfronts, flower baskets, and a surprising density of good cafes and restaurants for a town of this size. Mountains rise to the north and south, and the broad estuary of the Kenmare River stretches away to the west.

The town sits between two of Ireland's famous peninsulas, the Iveragh, with its Ring of Kerry, and the Beara, wilder and emptier. Kenmare is the natural base for both, and riders arrive from Killarney over the high road through the Moll's Gap, a fine climb with views over the mountains. There is also a prehistoric stone circle on the edge of town, one of the largest in the south-west of Ireland, with a boulder in the centre and a quiet, slightly eerie atmosphere. Kenmare is also known for its lace, which was made by nuns in the nineteenth century as a way of giving local women work.

For a motorcyclist, Kenmare is a fine place to rest and refuel. The town has pumps, shops, and plenty of places to eat, from pubs serving seafood chowder and brown bread to more ambitious restaurants. Fresh fish and shellfish from the bay are a highlight, and the local cheeses and lamb are excellent. The roads out of town are good, though the Ring of Kerry in summer can be crowded with coaches, and the narrow bends and blind corners need care. The Healy Pass on the Beara side is a spectacular alternative, with tight hairpins and a rougher surface.

Weather in Kerry is changeable, and rain can arrive at any moment, so carry a waterproof layer and expect a mix of sun and showers in a single afternoon. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with fewer crowds and clear light, while summer brings long evenings but more traffic. Cill Airne, the Irish name for Killarney, is the bigger town about twenty kilometres to the north-east. Kenmare itself has all you need, and the pace of life is unhurried.
t.wicklow gap@53.0,-6.4:
The Wicklow Gap is Ireland's idea of a mountain pass, which is to say it is modest in height and enormous in mood. The road climbs out of the Glendasan valley onto bare, peat-brown moorland, with the long shoulders of the Wicklow Mountains rolling away on either side, and at the top the world opens into a high, empty bowl of heather, grass, and wind. Clouds move across it fast, and on a grey day the whole scene has a Scandinavian bleakness that is hard to match elsewhere in the country.

The mountains here are granite, and they are among the oldest in Ireland, shaped by ice and worn smooth. The valley below the gap holds Lough Nahanagan, a dark glacial tarn, and beyond it lies Glendalough, the monastic city founded by Saint Kevin in the sixth century. Its round tower and ruined churches stand beside two lakes in a wooded glen, and they are among the most evocative early Christian sites in Europe. On the hillside at Turlough, a pumped storage power station uses a reservoir that sits on the top of a mountain, an odd piece of engineering in an otherwise wild landscape.

The riding on the R756 is a pleasure when the weather behaves. The climb from the Glendalough side is steady, with bends that tighten and open and a surface that has improved in recent years, though frost and water can leave patches. The descent toward Hollywood and the Blessington lakes is longer and straighter, with fine views over the reservoirs. Sheep wander across the road, and fog can arrive in minutes, so keep your speed under control and your visor clean. Weekend traffic includes cyclists and walkers, particularly in summer.

Blessington, about seventeen kilometres to the north-east, is the nearest sizeable town with stations and shops, and Rathdrum and Valleymount are smaller places in the area. Carry a waterproof layer whatever the forecast, because wind and rain are likely, and a hot drink in Laragh or Glendalough before or after the pass is an excellent idea. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with clearer light and fewer crowds. In winter, snow and ice make the gap treacherous, and it is sometimes closed.
t.laragh food@53.0,-6.3:
Laragh is a small village in the heart of the Wicklow Mountains, at the junction of several valleys, and a natural place to stop for a meal. It sits a short distance from Glendalough, the Glen of the Two Lakes, where Saint Kevin founded a monastery in the sixth century. The remains are still there: a tall round tower, about thirty metres high, a roofless cathedral, small stone churches and a graveyard of Celtic crosses, all set beside dark lakes under steep, wooded slopes. For centuries, it was one of the great pilgrimage sites of Ireland, and in good weather it is still a gentle and moving place to walk.

For food, Laragh has a handful of pubs and cafés, and the habit of the place is to eat hearty. Expect a bowl of soup, brown bread, a toasted sandwich and a pot of tea, or something heavier with a pint. In summer, tables fill early and the car park overflows, so aim for a weekday and a mid-morning arrival. In winter, the place is quiet and the fires are lit.

The riding around Laragh is some of the best in eastern Ireland. The Wicklow Gap road climbs west from the valley to a high, bare saddle at roughly 480 metres, where heather moor, bog and grey rock stretch away on either side, and the bends are open and flowing. To the north, the Military Road, built by the British after the 1798 rebellion to flush out rebels hiding in the hills, runs along the high moorland past Sally Gap, with long straights, big views and sheep wandering across the tarmac. The surface can be rough in places, with frost damage and gravel, and the weather is wet and changeable, with low cloud and sudden showers. Fog can close in quickly on the high ground. Traffic is heavy on summer weekends and calm during the week.

The mountains are the largest upland area in Ireland, a granite massif with peat bogs, deer, and a national park. The smell of turf smoke and wet heather is part of the experience.

For fuel, do not rely on Laragh. Rathdrum, about ten kilometres away, and Wicklow town, a bit farther, have petrol stations, and it is safest to fill up there before heading into the hills. Eat well, wear a waterproof, and go up the gap in the afternoon light.
t.devoran and perran@50.2,-5.1:
Devoran is a quiet village at the head of Restronguet Creek, a tidal arm of the Fal estuary south of Truro, and it takes a little imagination to see it as the busy industrial port it once was. In the nineteenth century, the Redruth and Chasewater Railway brought copper ore down from the mines to quays here, where ships loaded it for smelters in South Wales and returned with coal. The remains of the quays, ore hoppers and old warehouses are still visible along the shore, and the village is part of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape, listed by UNESCO in 2006.

Up the valley at Perranarworthal, the Perran Foundry built massive steam engines that pumped water from mines across Cornwall and beyond, and its granite buildings still stand beside the road. The tidal creek, once choked with silt from the mines upstream, is now a peaceful haven for wading birds, with egrets and curlews feeding in the mud at low tide. The Mineral Tramways path follows the old railway line inland, a pleasant walk or ride for cyclists through woods and mining country.

The riding is classic Cornish lanes: narrow, high-hedged, twisting and often only one vehicle wide, with occasional passing places and unexpected tractors. The A39 between Truro and Falmouth runs past nearby and is busy in summer, but the side roads along the creek and towards Mylor and Feock reward a gentle pace with glimpses of water and boats. The King Harry chain ferry across the Fal is a lovely shortcut to the Roseland peninsula. The weather changes quickly, and the lanes are often damp and muddy, especially in autumn and winter.

Penryn, a few kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés, as does the busier town of Falmouth beyond. Devoran has a pub and a village shop, and the creekside is a good place to stop for a pasty, the miners' traditional lunch, with crimped edges that they reputedly used as a handle and threw away to avoid arsenic-laced fingers. Look out for the old ore hoppers and imagine the clatter of wagons and the masts of ships crowding the tiny harbour.
t.archaeological site of volubilis@34.1,-5:
Olive trees have surrounded Volubilis for two thousand years, and they still do. The Roman city, on a gentle slope below the Zerhoun massif north of Meknes, was the westernmost major town of the empire's province of Mauretania Tingitana, and it grew rich on olive oil, grain and the trade in wild animals for the arenas of Rome. Its ruins include a triumphal arch dedicated to the emperor Caracalla, a basilica, a forum, temples, and above all a series of houses with superb mosaics in their floors, showing Orpheus with his lyre, the labours of Hercules, Bacchus and Diana bathing. Volubilis became a World Heritage Site in 1997.

After the Romans withdrew, the city lived on, and in the late eighth century Idris I, founder of the first Moroccan dynasty, came here and was proclaimed ruler. His tomb lies in the holy town of Moulay Idriss Zerhoun, a few kilometres away, whose white houses tumble down two hills, an important pilgrimage site for Moroccans.

The landscape around Volubilis is green in spring, with wheat, olives and wildflowers, and the views from the site over the plain toward the hills are wide and lovely. Storks nest on the columns of the basilica. In summer, the heat is intense, and there is little shade on the site, so come early or late.

The riding is pleasant: the roads from Meknes to Volubilis and Moulay Idriss wind through hills and olive groves, with good surfaces and moderate traffic. The road over the Zerhoun mountains is narrower and more scenic. Watch for donkeys, carts, pedestrians and grand taxis stopping without warning. Further north, the roads toward the Rif and Chefchaouen are spectacular.

Meknes, twenty kilometres away, is the place to top up the tank, and it is a fine imperial city in its own right, built by Sultan Moulay Ismail. Fez is an hour east. Near the site, small restaurants serve tagines and grilled meat, and the local olive oil is excellent.
t.the port of hayle@50.2,-5.4:
Hayle does not look like much at first: a long, low town strung along an estuary, a scatter of industrial buildings, quays slowly silting up and a lot of sand. But in the nineteenth century this was one of the engine rooms of the world. Two great foundries here, Harvey's and the Copperhouse company, built the steam engines that pumped water out of Cornish mines and later out of mines and waterworks on several continents. The harbour shipped copper ore out and coal in, and the whole place is part of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape World Heritage site.

Walk along the quays and you will see the bones of that past: granite wharves, the long footbridge over the old sluicing pools that kept the harbour clear, and the restored buildings of Harvey's foundry. The engines built here were enormous, with cylinders big enough to stand in, and they were shipped across the world, including to the Netherlands to help drain the Haarlemmermeer polder.

The estuary is now a nature reserve, a favourite haunt of birders who come for waders, gulls, egrets and winter visitors in large numbers. Beyond it, the Towans, a long line of sand dunes, stretch along St Ives Bay to Godrevy Point, where the lighthouse inspired Virginia Woolf's novel To the Lighthouse. Seals haul out on the beaches below Godrevy, and the sunsets over St Ives on the far side of the bay are glorious.

The riding in West Cornwall is a mixed bag. The A30 is busy and uninspiring, but the coastal roads are narrow, twisty and often lined with high hedges, which makes them fun but blind. Expect tractors, camper vans and holiday traffic in summer, and do not trust a satnav that sends you down a single-track lane with grass in the middle. Spring and early autumn are the sweet spot: warm enough, less crowded, and the light on the sea is beautiful.

Hayle has fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat. A Cornish pasty from a local bakery is almost mandatory, and Hayle has a couple of bakers with strong local followings. St Ives, five kilometres away, is busier and prettier, with a Tate gallery and narrow streets, but parking is a nightmare, so leave the bike at the edge of town.
t.st just mining district@50.1,-5.7:
Out at the very end of Cornwall, where the land runs out in granite cliffs above the Atlantic, the coast between St Just and Pendeen is studded with the ruined engine houses of tin and copper mines. Some of them stand right on the cliff edge, their tall chimneys silhouetted against the sea, and the shafts below ran out under the ocean floor, so deep that miners claimed they could hear boulders rolling on the seabed above them during storms. This is the St Just Mining District, one of the most dramatic parts of the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape World Heritage site.

The names are evocative: Botallack, with its Crowns engine houses perched on a rock ledge just above the waves; Levant, where a restored beam engine still puffs into life under steam; and Geevor, the last mine in the area to close, in 1990, now a museum where you can go underground. The Levant mine was also the scene of a terrible disaster in 1919, when the man engine that carried miners up and down the shaft collapsed, killing thirty-one men. The landscape was the backdrop for the television series Poldark, and fans come to see the locations.

The riding here is some of the best in Cornwall. The B3306 coast road from St Ives to St Just is a classic, winding through moorland, granite boulders and tiny villages, with the Atlantic on one side and the high ground of Penwith on the other. It is narrow, with tight bends, stone walls and blind crests, and in summer it can be busy with tourists, so ride early or late. Watch for livestock, walkers and cyclists, and be ready for fog rolling in from the sea at any time.

Penwith is ancient country. Beyond the mines, the moors are scattered with standing stones, stone circles, burial chambers and Iron Age villages like Chysauster and Carn Euny. The cliffs are home to choughs, the red-billed crows that are a symbol of Cornwall, and seals and dolphins are often seen offshore. Cape Cornwall, just west of St Just, is a headland with a single chimney on top and wonderful views.

St Just, about two and a half kilometres away, is a small granite town with shops, pubs and cafés, and a petrol station on its outskirts. Penzance, about ten kilometres away, is the main town with all services. A pint in a granite pub and a crab sandwich in a harbour café are the way to finish the day here.
t.trewavas@50.1,-5.4:
Trewavas Head is a short stretch of Cornish cliff, between Porthleven and Marazion, where the old engine houses of Wheal Trewavas cling to the rocks above the sea. The mine, which worked tin and copper in the nineteenth century, was dug from the cliff face and went out under the sea bed, and its engine houses were built in a precarious position on ledges with the Atlantic breaking below. The sight is one of the most dramatic in the Cornish mining landscape, which UNESCO listed in 2006, and the story of the miners who worked there, hanging on the cliffs and tunnelling under the waves, is told in the old photographs.

The coast is rocky and wild, with granite and greenstone cliffs, small coves and a view along the bay to St Michael's Mount, the tidal island with its castle and chapel on a rock. The Cornish names, Trewavas, Praa Sands, Porthleven, speak of an older language. Gorse and heather flower on the clifftops, and in spring the banks are full of sea pinks and bluebells. Grey seals can be seen from the cliffs, and the sea has a green and violet colour on a bright day.

Cornish lanes are narrow, hedged and often sunken, and a motorcycle is a good way to get through them, though they demand care. Corners are blind, the surface is rough, and tractors and holiday traffic are common in July and August. Porthleven, a small harbour town on the coast, has a fine harbour with a clock tower, and Helston, a bigger market town, hosts the Flora Day each May, when the streets are filled with dancing. Fuel is available in Helston, the nearest large town, and in Porthleven.

For the best experience, come in spring or early autumn, when the weather is mild, and the crowds are thin. Storms in winter can be violent, with waves breaking over the cliffs, and the paths may be closed. Take care near the cliff edge, and keep to the paths, because old mine shafts are hidden in the gorse.
t.portreath branch of the hayle railway@50:
Cornwall's first railways were built to carry copper ore down to the sea and coal back up, and the Portreath branch of the Hayle Railway was one of the busiest. It opened in 1837, joining the mines around Redruth to the small harbour at Portreath on the north coast, where ore was loaded onto ships bound for the smelters of south Wales, and coal came in to feed the pumping engines. A tramroad had already done the same job here since the early nineteenth century, and the railway replaced it with steam power and heavier loads.

The line is now a path, part of the Great Flat Lode and Coast-to-Coast trails, and one of the elements of the Cornish Mining Landscape that UNESCO listed in 2006. Walking or cycling it, you pass engine houses, spoil heaps, old stamps and the dips and cuttings where the track ran, all slowly being reclaimed by gorse and bracken. Some of the engine houses look like small churches, tall granite chimneys beside roofless sheds with big arched openings where the great beam engines once stood. The whole landscape is scattered with them, and it is the sheer number that sinks in.

Portreath itself is a pretty little place, a steep-sided cove with a harbour, a beach and a surf school, and a row of cottages tumbling down the hill. The sea can be rough here, and storms throw spray over the harbour wall. The coast to the west and east is cliffs, caves and rocky coves where seals haul out in autumn.

The roads in this part of Cornwall are narrow, bending and frequently bordered by high banks and hedges, so visibility is short and you should be ready to meet a tractor around every corner. The B3300 coast road is the best, with sea views and a mix of tight and open bends, but it gets crowded on summer weekends, when visitors fill every parking space. Early morning or late afternoon is better. Spring is bright and often breezy, and winter gales can be wild.

Redruth, two and a half kilometres away, has forty thousand people and offers fuel, supermarkets and cafés. A Cornish pasty from a village bakery is the traditional rider's lunch.
Pool is the place where Cornwall's mining past is easiest to see, because it lies along the main road between Camborne and Redruth, and the engine houses are right beside it. East Pool Mine, now cared for by the National Trust, was one of the richest tin mines in the county, and it kept working until 1945. Two huge beam engines still stand under their roofs, and the big granite engine house, with its tall chimney and arched openings, dominates the village. It is one of the sites that make up the Cornish Mining Landscape, inscribed by UNESCO in 2006.

The industry that grew up here was global. Cornish engineers designed pumping and winding engines that were used in mines from Mexico to Australia, and Cornish miners, known as Cousin Jacks, carried their skills and their pasties to every continent. Richard Trevithick, who lived in nearby Camborne, built one of the first steam road vehicles in 1801 and drove it up Camborne Hill, an event still celebrated in the town every April. The great engines at Pool are among the survivors of that age.

Close by, the Heartlands centre, a former mine site converted into gardens and exhibitions, gives you a feel for the world of the miners. Camborne's School of Mines trained generations of engineers, and the town still has an air of practical, workmanlike pride. The small terraced houses and Methodist chapels, plain and sturdy, belong to the same story, since Methodism took root deeply among Cornish miners.

The country around is not dramatic but intriguing. The ground is scarred by the old workings, and the fields are scattered with stone ruins, but the scenery is open and the light is bright. The coast, a few kilometres north, offers wild cliffs and good beaches. The A30 runs past on its way to Penzance, and you want to get off it quickly onto the minor roads, which are narrower and slower but more rewarding.

Camborne is the place for fuel, supermarkets and cafés, with twenty-two thousand people and three kilometres to go. Opening times of the engine houses vary by season, so check before you arrive. Bring a waterproof, since the Cornish weather changes fast.
t.st agnes mining district@50.3,-5.2:
St Agnes is a village of fewer than three thousand people on the north coast of Cornwall, and its coastline is one of the most photographed in the county. The reason is Wheal Coates, a pair of engine houses perched on a cliff above the sea at Chapel Porth, the sort of view that appears on tea towels. The engine houses once pumped water from tin and copper mines that ran under the cliff, and miners worked in tunnels that went out beneath the waves. Today they stand roofless, with ferns in the windows, against a sky that seems to change every few minutes.

The St Agnes mining district is among the places that make up the Cornish Mining Landscape, listed by UNESCO in 2006. From the high point of the district, St Agnes Beacon, about two hundred metres up, you can see the coast curve away on either side and the old workings spread inland. In the nineteenth century this was an industrial landscape, full of smoke and noise, and it is strange to imagine it now, when the only sounds are gulls, wind and the occasional walker.

The village has a solid granite centre of small shops, pubs and chapels, and a steep road down to Trevaunance Cove, a small beach with a long history of failed attempts to build a harbour. Storms smashed them time after time. The coast path from St Agnes to Chapel Porth is among the best short walks in Cornwall, with views over the sea and old mine ruins on every hill.

The roads in this area are small and winding. The B3285 and the coast road are narrow, with sharp bends and little room to pass, and in summer they get congested. The beach at Chapel Porth has limited parking, and you should expect delays. Early spring and autumn are quieter, with sharp light on the sea, and winter storms can be dramatic. Gravel, sand and mud on the road are common.

Fuel may be limited in the village, so fill up at Redruth, nine kilometres away, with forty thousand people and all the usual services. A pasty from a local baker and a drink at a pub with a fire make a good way to end the day.
t.marrakech@31.6,-8.0:
Marrakech announces itself with a smell before it shows its face: woodsmoke, orange blossom, leather, grilled meat, with mint and diesel in the mix. The city, founded in the later eleventh century by the Almoravids, grew from a camp of tents at the edge of the Haouz plain into the capital of a series of Berber dynasties. Its walls and many of its buildings are built of local red clay, giving it the nickname of the red city, and behind them sits the old medina, a maze of lanes where mopeds, donkey carts and tourists push through together. The Koutoubia mosque, whose minaret rises about seventy metres above the roofs and dates from the twelfth century, is the landmark you steer by.

Jemaa el-Fna, the great square at the medina's heart, wakes up in the late afternoon, when food stalls roll out and the smoke begins to rise, and storytellers, musicians and snake charmers draw their circles of onlookers. It is theatre, and it is also a place to eat well: grilled lamb, harira soup, and fresh orange juice for little money. For something quieter, the Majorelle garden, with its cobalt-blue walls, and the old madrasa of Ben Youssef, offer relief from the noise.

For a rider, Marrakech is the doorway to the High Atlas. The Tizi n'Tichka pass, at 2,260 metres, carries the N9 road over the mountains to Ouarzazate, with a long, steady climb through red hills, then a series of hairpins, tunnels of cloud and views over terraced villages with flat-roofed houses. It is the main route to the south, so it is shared with trucks, buses and shared taxis, which overtake with confidence, and the surface can be broken at the edges. In winter, snow and ice can close it for hours, and the weather changes fast, so look at the forecast. Start early, because the mountain air gets bumpy and cold by the afternoon, and the descent toward the desert side is dry and bright.

Marrakech is a city of more than eight hundred thousand people, so fuel and workshops are easy to find, and the main stations are along the ring roads. Town riding is wild, with scooters appearing from every side, so ride defensively and park the bike in a guarded lot. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summer heat can top forty degrees, and the cold nights of winter can surprise you. Take some cash, and agree on prices first.
t.wheal peevor@50.3,-5.2:
Cornwall's mining country does not look like postcards. Around Redruth the land is brown and scrubby, with chimneys and roofless engine houses standing on every hill, and the soil still carries scars where shafts and spoil heaps once covered the countryside. Wheal Peevor is one of those engine houses, near the village of St Day, and a small piece of what UNESCO recognised as the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape. At its peak in the nineteenth century, Cornwall produced a huge share of the world's copper and tin, and Cornish miners and engineers carried their skills to Australia, South Africa, Mexico and the United States, which is why you find Cornish pasties in places far from Cornwall.

The site is a short walk from the road, with a free-to-visit engine house, boiler house and chimney in a heathy landscape where gorse and heather grow over old spoil. The place is wonderfully atmospheric in low evening light, when the stone turns gold and the wind sings through the empty windows. Take care around old workings, which are real hazards, and keep to the paths.

The riding in this part of Cornwall is a mixture of narrow lanes, busy A-roads and flat coastal stretches. The A30 passes close by and brings holiday traffic in summer, so I prefer the back roads, which wind through granite villages with Methodist chapels on every corner. Surfaces are generally fine, but the lanes can be narrow, steep and walled, and tractors are common. Weather arrives off the Atlantic with little warning, so expect mist, drizzle and sudden brightness in the same hour.

Redruth, about two kilometres away, is a large town of over forty thousand with all the usual shops, supermarkets, petrol stations and cafés, so food and fuel are no problem. It is a slightly faded place, but with a strong sense of identity. Nearby are the Great Flat Lode trail, the Mineral Tramways, and the north coast at Portreath and Porthtowan, where the cliffs drop to surf beaches and the wind blows hard.

For lunch, a pasty is the obvious choice, a food that was invented as a portable meal for miners, with a crimped crust that served as a handle and was discarded because arsenic from the ore could contaminate it. That, at least, is the story, and it has been told over a great many pasties.
t.taddert@31.4,-7.4:
Taddert is a small village strung along the N9 high in the Atlas, a few hundred metres below the Tizi n'Tichka pass, which at around twenty-two hundred and sixty metres is the highest main road crossing of the range. Every vehicle that makes the journey between Marrakech and Ouarzazate comes through, so the village has a lively roadside life, with cafés, mineral and fossil shops, and men waving at passing riders. Fuel is available, which helps, because the climb on both sides is long.

The road itself was built in the 1930s by the French and has been repaired and widened many times since. It climbs from Marrakech in a series of broad bends, with long, steep gradients and hairpins that drag trucks to a crawl, and this makes overtaking a daily challenge. Rock falls and potholes are common, and mist, rain and snow in winter can close the pass or demand chains. Between December and March, check conditions before you go. In the early morning, with a clear sky and cold air, the descent towards the desert side is wonderful.

Around Taddert, the landscape changes dramatically. The northern slopes are green with walnut and almond groves, and the villages are built of terracotta-coloured mud brick. After the pass, the colours turn to red and ochre, and the valleys are dry and wide. A few kilometres off the main road, the kasbah at Telouet, once the seat of the powerful Glaoui family, who ruled the region under the French, stands in crumbling splendour with its painted ceilings still visible.

Practical advice is simple. Fill your tank here or in Ouarzazate, bring cash in dirhams, and buy water. Mint tea at a roadside café is a good rest, though the sweetness may surprise you. Beware of dogs, goats and children near the road, and of lorries cutting corners. Bargaining is the norm in the shops, and a smile goes a long way. Spring and autumn offer the best weather, while summer is hot on the southern side.
t.ait benhaddou@31.0,-7.1:
Aït Benhaddou looks like a sandcastle that someone left to harden for four hundred years. The ksar, a fortified village of rammed-earth towers and flat-roofed houses stacked up a hillside above the Ounila river, sits about thirty kilometres from Ouarzazate on the old caravan track between the Sahara and Marrakech, and it was listed by UNESCO in 1987. The walls glow red-ochre in the evening, the towers have geometric patterns pressed into their upper storeys, and the whole cluster is reflected, on the rare days when the river runs full, in the water below.

The place is a monument to the trade that made it. Caravans carrying salt, gold, slaves and cloth came up from Timbuktu and across the desert, and this was a stop where merchants rested before crossing the High Atlas by the Tizi n'Tichka. Today only a handful of families still live inside the old walls, while most of the village has moved across the river into modern houses, and the earth buildings need constant repair after rain. Cinema found it early. Lawrence of Arabia, Gladiator and the Game of Thrones series all used it, which explains the souvenir shops and the camels waiting for hire.

For a rider, the approach is the thing. The N9 descends from Taddert in long, broad curves into a drier, redder landscape, with the road dropping toward the Ouarzazate basin in stages and the colour of the rock changing from brown to a deep brick. A short side road leads to the ksar from the main highway, and the surface is generally fine. Morning or late afternoon light is best for both riding and photographs, since the midday sun flattens everything, and in July and August the heat is considerable.

Small cafés on the river bank serve mint tea and tagine, and you can cross the river on stepping stones or, when the water is high, on a small footbridge. Keep some cash for the entry to the upper terraces, which usually costs a few dirhams, and wear shoes with a decent grip, because the paths are steep and loose. Go before the tour buses, if you can manage it.
t.essaouira@31.5,-9.8:
The wind is the first thing you meet in Essaouira, and it never really leaves. The trade winds blow in from the Atlantic for most of the year, which is why the old Portuguese-named town of Mogador is a centre for windsurfing and kitesurfing, and why the beach is a long, flat plain of pale sand with surfers working the surf at the far end. The pin sits just outside the medina, about a kilometre from the town centre, and the air smells of salt, grilled fish and woodsmoke from the carpenters' workshops.

The walled town was laid out in the late eighteenth century for the Moroccan sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah, who wanted a port to rival Agadir and attract European trade. A French engineer, Théodore Cornut, is generally credited with the plan, which is why the streets run in straight lines, unusual for a Moroccan medina. UNESCO listed it in 2001. Black brass cannons still point out to sea from the ramparts of the Skala, where the waves slam into the rocks and the gulls ride the updraughts. t.ksar of ait ben haddou@31.0,-7.1:

t.limerick@52.7,-8.6:

Choose a hotel with secure parking, as is common in the city centre. t.cork@51.9,-8.5:

t.taroudant@30.5,-8.9:

t.l archipel d essaouira@31.5,-9.8:

A walk along the beach at low tide, with the islets silhouetted against the setting sun, is a fine end to the ride. t.medina of essaouira@31.5,-9.8:

t.medina of marrakesh@31.6,-8.0:
Marrakesh began as a camp. In about 1070, the Almoravids, a Berber dynasty from the Sahara, pitched their tents on this plain at the foot of the High Atlas and began to build a city, and within a century it was the capital of an empire that stretched from Spain to Senegal. Marrakesh is a big city of over eight hundred thousand with fuel at every turn, so fill before leaving. Try a tagine, a bowl of harira soup, or an orange juice from the stalls at the square, and sit on a rooftop terrace at sunset to watch the lights come on. Summer is very hot, and spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.medina et le jardin d agdal@31.6,-8.0:
The Agdal Gardens are a vast orchard on the southern edge of Marrakesh, a rectangle of olive, orange, pomegranate and apricot trees that stretches for about three kilometres behind high red walls. The channels, called khettaras, carry meltwater from the High Atlas to the city underground, protected from evaporation, and a network of basins, canals and sluices distributes it through the gardens. Without them, Marrakesh could not have grown, and the oasis would not exist. Try sea bream from the grill at the fish market, and a glass of mint tea at a cafe by the river. Spring is the most pleasant season, and the light at the end of the afternoon turns the tower gold.
t.mosquee de tengrela@10.5,-6.4:
Tengréla sits in the far north of Côte d'Ivoire, only a few kilometers from the border with Mali, in a landscape of dry savanna, cashew orchards and cotton fields. Trucks and local buses take up much of the road. The best season is the dry months from November to February, though the harmattan, a dusty wind from the Sahara, fills the air with haze and lowers visibility. The rainy season, from May to October, can turn dirt roads to mud.

Visitors should be respectful. The mosque is a living place of worship, so dress modestly, ask permission before entering and avoid prayer times. A local guide can explain the details and help with introductions.
t.sudanese style mosques in northern cote:
Across the savanna of northern Côte d'Ivoire stands a small family of mud mosques that look as if they were grown rather than built. Eight of them were inscribed together by UNESCO in 2021 as the Sudanese style mosques of the north, among them the mosques of Kong, Kawara, Sorobango, Samatiguila, Nambira and Tengréla. Thick walls of banco, a mix of clay and straw, lean inward as they rise, and rows of palm-wood beams stick out of the surface like the quills of a porcupine. Conical buttresses crowned with pinnacles line the facade, and the whole building is plastered smooth with fresh mud after each rainy season. The beams are both decoration and scaffolding, which means communities can climb up every year and renew the walls without building a frame. A mosque of this kind lasts only as long as the people around it keep caring for it, which is a rather lovely thing to know when you stand in front of one.

Tengréla lies close to the Mali border, in a land of cashew orchards, shea trees and cotton fields, and the roads between the mosque towns are a mix of decent tarmac and red laterite. The rains, from about May to October, turn tracks to slick mud and bring river crossings that you should not attempt lightly.

Services depend on the town. Tengréla, with some forty thousand people, has fuel, a market and basic places to sleep, but the smaller mosque villages may have little beyond a bench under a mango tree and cold water in a clay pot. Fill up before you leave Korhogo or Tengréla and carry water. Mosques are active places of worship, so dress modestly, ask permission and avoid the hours of prayer, particularly on Fridays.

A local guide is worth the small cost, because they can explain the caretaking traditions and make the introductions that open the door.
t.todra gorge@31.6,-5.6:
Todra Gorge is a slot in the High Atlas where the Todgha River has cut through red limestone, leaving walls that rise sheer, close to three hundred metres, on either side of a gap just wide enough for the road and the stream. The best time to visit is early morning, before the crowds and when the light is lowest, or late afternoon. t.ait oudinar@31.5,-5.9:

Past Ait Oudinar, the cliffs close in and the road begins a series of bends along the river, with villages tucked into side valleys and kasbahs standing on the ridges. Early morning is lovely, when the light is soft on the rock and the village is just waking up, while afternoons can be hot and dusty. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and winter brings cold nights and occasional snow in the high valleys.

t.dades hairpins@31.6,-5.9:
The Dades hairpins are Morocco's answer to a stack of pancakes: a series of tight switchbacks that climb the side of the gorge, with the road folding back on itself again and again as it gains height above the river. From the viewpoint at the top, the whole route lies below you like a ribbon dropped on rock, and the red-orange walls of the Dades Gorge fall away into the valley. The riding is short, sharp and satisfying. The road is narrow and steep, with tight bends, a gradient that makes you work the gearbox, and patches of rough surface where rain and frost have broken the edges. Trucks and tour vehicles use the road, and they can take a wide line on the corners, so stay to your side and keep your speed modest. In dry weather the surface is manageable, but after rain mud and gravel can wash across the bends. Go early in the morning for the best light and the fewest vehicles, and expect to stop at the viewpoint, because the view is hard to resist.

The valley has long been a route through the Atlas. Amazigh families farmed the narrow ribbon of land along the river, herders moved flocks to the high pastures, and caravans passed between the Draa valley and the oases of the south. The road itself, a modern construction, was built to link the gorge's villages and to open the area to travellers. Small cafes at the viewpoint serve mint tea and omelettes, and the owners are used to riders arriving with dust on their visors.

Ravens and choughs ride the updrafts, and in spring wildflowers appear on the slopes. The air smells of dry earth, thyme and wood smoke, and the silence is broken only by the occasional engine.

t.tizi ntichka@31.3,-7.4:
Tizi n'Tichka, at about 2,260 metres, is the highest main road pass in Morocco, and for centuries it has been the route that carries Marrakech across the High Atlas toward the desert. The N9 climbs steadily from the plain through red earth, pine and juniper, with roadside stalls selling geodes, fossils and amethyst crystals, before reaching the crest, where a modest sign and a row of tea shops mark the top. Midday heat in summer on the southern slope is another matter.

t.tizi ntest@30.9,-8.4:
Tizi n'Test is the pass that makes riders go quiet, then talk about it for years. At about 2,090 metres, it crosses the High Atlas between Marrakech and the Souss plain near Taroudant, and the road, built by the French in the late 1920s and early 1930s, is a thin ribbon of tarmac cut into the mountainside, with hairpins, drops of several hundred metres, and, in places, no barrier at all. It is narrow, in sections just wide enough for two vehicles to squeeze past, and landslides and rockfall are part of life.

The charm is in the detail. South of Ouirgane, the road climbs through valleys of walnut and almond trees, then follows a series of switchbacks to the top, where a café sits beside the road, and then it drops in long, curving descents toward the arid country around Taroudant. The view back across the valleys and ridges is wonderful, and in clear weather the Atlas looks endless. Near the pass, the ruins of the Tin Mal mosque, built in the twelfth century, mark the origin of the Almohad dynasty that went on to rule Morocco and much of Spain, and it is among the few mosques in Morocco open to non-Muslim visitors.

Snow and rain can close it in winter, and even in good weather heavy lorries and tourist coaches slow the traffic, often stopping on bends, and some surfaces are rough, with gravel on the edges. Aim to cross in the morning, in dry weather, and keep to your side of the road, since oncoming vehicles tend to cut corners. Fog is possible, and darkness makes the pass far more dangerous.

There is no town near the summit, so plan your fuel properly. Fill the tank in Marrakech or Taroudant, since small villages along the route may have little or nothing, and carry water and snacks. A simple stop for mint tea, bread and olive oil at the café near the top will give you time to settle your nerves before the descent. Early spring brings wildflowers and green slopes, while autumn gives the clearest light.
t.dades gorge@31.5,-5.9:

The road through the gorge is a joy for riders who like a challenge. It climbs along the river, with the cliffs towering above, before a famous series of tight hairpins zigzags up a steep slope, tarmac stacked above tarmac like a staircase, with a viewpoint above where you can look back down the whole sequence. Beyond that, the road gets rougher and narrower as it penetrates further into the mountains, and sections may be damaged by floods, which are sudden and severe after storms. Sun comes late in the narrow valley, so mornings are cool, and the light on the rock at the end of the day is wonderful.

Spring is the best season, when almond blossom and green barley contrast with red rock, and the road is dry. Summer midday is hot and the cliffs hold the heat, while winter nights are cold and snow can block upper stretches. Do not ride the gorge in heavy rain, because flash floods and rockfall are real hazards.

Nearby Kelaat M'Gouna is known for roses, which are grown in hedges around the fields and turned into rosewater and cosmetics, and celebrated with a festival each spring. The nearest big town is Tinghir, about thirty-seven kilometres to the east, which is where to fill the tank and buy supplies, along with Kelaat M'Gouna, as the guesthouses in the gorge are small and fuel is not guaranteed. t.imilchil@32.2,-5.6:

Allihies is a village of painted houses at the western tip of the Beara peninsula, and it has an unlikely history. In the nineteenth century this remote corner was the centre of a copper mining boom, and Cornish miners came to work the mines under the Puxley family, bringing their skills, their Methodism and their names. The chimneys and engine houses of the old mines still stand on the hillside above the village, empty and photogenic in a bleak way, and the houses of the miners are painted in yellow, blue, pink and green.

The mine closed in the 1880s, and many of the families emigrated, some to America and some to Australia, and the village has never quite recovered its former size. A small museum in a former church tells the story, with displays of mining equipment and photographs, and the Cornish connection is still recalled with affection. On the beach below the village the sand has a golden colour and a peculiar texture, partly the product of mining waste ground by the sea.

The ride here is a delight. The road from Castletownbere runs west along the southern shore of the peninsula in tight bends, rising and falling with the contours, with views of the sea and the islands, and the final run to the village crosses an open, windswept moor. It is narrow, with stone walls, sheep and cattle grids, and a surface that is generally good but can be rough in places. At the very end of the peninsula, a road leads to Dursey Sound, where Ireland's only cable car carries passengers over the water to Dursey Island.

Nature is spectacular. The moors are covered with heather and gorse, the cliffs are home to seabirds, and gannets plunge into the sea offshore. Whales and dolphins are sometimes seen from the headlands, and the light on the Atlantic is extraordinary. The air has a salty tang with a hint of turf smoke.

The village has a few pubs, cafes and places to stay, but a larger range of services is at Castletownbere, about fifteen kilometres back along the road. Walk up to the mine buildings, and look out across the ocean.

The middle of the Wicklow plateau is a strange place to try to describe, because it is mostly absence. These coordinates sit in the upland between Sally Gap and Laragh, where the Military Road crosses heather moor, drops toward the Glenmacnass valley and passes under slopes that are brown for most of the year and purple for about three weeks in late summer. Valleymount to the west and Rathdrum to the south are the nearest named places, and both are a long way off by road. You are, for practical purposes, alone with the weather.

Descending toward Glenmacnass is the best part. The road tips down into a glacial valley, a classic U shape carved by ice, and the waterfall that tumbles beside the road in the upper valley is one of the few places on the route where almost everybody stops. Pull off carefully; the lay-by is small and the road above it has fast, blind approaches. After rain the falls are loud enough to hear through a helmet, and in a dry August they dwindle to a rope of white water on dark rock.

The Military Road was built in the aftermath of the 1798 rising to give the army access to the glens where rebel bands had hidden. Construction took years, and the line it follows through the mountains is deliberately direct, which is why it feels more like an engineer's decision than a traveller's. Barracks were placed at intervals, and a few survive in one form or another. The rebels lost the war, but the road gave the area its first real link to the outside world, and the glens slowly opened.

Riding it is easy but never dull. Corners are open and readable, the gradients are moderate, and the surface changes from smooth to patched without warning, usually just where a stream crosses underneath. In cold weather and low sun, black ice can sit in the shaded hollows long after the rest of the road has dried, so be cautious in the early mornings of spring and autumn.

For fuel and food, Rathdrum is the nearest small town, and Kilquade, farther east, is a bigger settlement. Laragh, down the valley, has cafes and a bakery-style stop where walkers and riders swap weather reports.
